lessons.title: Values, Types, Comparisons, and Control Flow
lessons.summary: JavaScript has primitive values and objects; variables bind names to values.
lessons.body:
Values, Types, Comparisons, and Control Flow

Why this matters
JavaScript has primitive values and objects; variables bind names to values. This lesson is intentionally framework-light. You are building a mental model that will be reused when Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, TanStack Query, and deployment tooling add more vocabulary. The goal is not to memorize definitions. The goal is to predict what the computer will do and know where to look when reality differs from that prediction.

Mental model
• JavaScript has primitive values and objects; variables bind names to values.
• Strict equality avoids coercion surprises in most application code.
• Truthy/falsy rules are useful but should not replace explicit domain checks when 0, empty string, or false are valid data.
• if/switch/loops express decisions; readable control flow is more valuable than clever one-liners.

Step-by-step walkthrough
1. Write the concept in your own words before using a tool. If your explanation depends on framework jargon, simplify it one level.
2. Create the smallest runnable example that demonstrates only this concept. Keep it outside the main TaskFlow repository if experimentation could create noise.
3. Predict the result before running the command or clicking the UI. Prediction makes the output evidence instead of entertainment.
4. Run it and capture what actually happened: terminal output, browser state, request details, or file changes.
5. Change one assumption and repeat. Try an invalid input, wrong path, missing field, reordered data, or other safe failure relevant to the topic.
6. Explain the difference between the successful and failing runs. That explanation is the transferable skill.

TaskFlow connection
Later in the course, javascript foundations i stops being an isolated topic and becomes infrastructure for real features. When you encounter values, types, comparisons, and control flow again, ask which layer owns it, what its inputs are, what output proves success, and what failure evidence is available. That prevents you from copying framework snippets without understanding the underlying browser, runtime, operating-system, or language behavior.

Guided exercise
Create a tiny example from scratch without copying the final code from a tutorial. Keep the example under about 30–50 lines where possible. After it works, deliberately break one assumption. Write the exact symptom and the smallest fix. Then delete the experiment or commit it in a dedicated practice folder so it does not pollute production project structure.

Check your understanding
• Can you describe the concept without naming a framework?
• Can you point to the exact input and output?
• Can you name one common incorrect assumption?
• Can you reproduce the idea in a tiny example?
• Can you diagnose one intentional failure using evidence rather than guesses?

Instructor note
Do not rush because the syntax looks easy. Most difficult full-stack bugs are not caused by forgetting syntax; they come from an incorrect model of ownership, execution environment, identity, time, or data flow. The foundation track exists so later lessons can move quickly without becoming mysterious.

lessons.title: Functions, Scope, Closures, and Callbacks
lessons.summary: Functions are values that can receive inputs and return outputs; small pure functions are easy to reason about and test.
lessons.body:
Functions, Scope, Closures, and Callbacks

Why this matters
Functions are values that can receive inputs and return outputs; small pure functions are easy to reason about and test. This lesson is intentionally framework-light. You are building a mental model that will be reused when Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, TanStack Query, and deployment tooling add more vocabulary. The goal is not to memorize definitions. The goal is to predict what the computer will do and know where to look when reality differs from that prediction.

Mental model
• Functions are values that can receive inputs and return outputs; small pure functions are easy to reason about and test.
• Lexical scope determines which bindings a function can access.
• Closures let functions retain access to surrounding values and power event handlers, factories, and framework hooks.
• Callbacks are simply functions passed to other functions; async APIs later build on the same idea.

lessons.title: Arrays, Objects, Destructuring, and Collection Methods
lessons.summary: Objects group named properties; arrays represent ordered collections.
lessons.body:
Arrays, Objects, Destructuring, and Collection Methods

Why this matters
Objects group named properties; arrays represent ordered collections. This lesson is intentionally framework-light. You are building a mental model that will be reused when Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, TanStack Query, and deployment tooling add more vocabulary. The goal is not to memorize definitions. The goal is to predict what the computer will do and know where to look when reality differs from that prediction.

Mental model
• Objects group named properties; arrays represent ordered collections.
• map transforms, filter selects, find locates one item, some/every answer predicates, and reduce accumulates when the operation genuinely fits.
• Destructuring can clarify which fields a function cares about, but over-nested destructuring can reduce readability.
• Prefer transformations that make data flow obvious over mutation scattered across many statements.

lessons.summary: const prevents rebinding, not mutation of an object.
lessons.body:
Mutation, Immutability, and Copying Data

Why this matters
const prevents rebinding, not mutation of an object. This lesson is intentionally framework-light. • const prevents rebinding, not mutation of an object.

lessons.summary: Modules give files explicit public imports/exports and reduce accidental global coupling.
lessons.body:
ES Modules, Errors, and Small Program Structure

Why this matters
Modules give files explicit public imports/exports and reduce accidental global coupling. This lesson is intentionally framework-light. You are building a mental model that will be reused when Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, TanStack Query, and deployment tooling add more vocabulary. The goal is not to memorize definitions. The goal is to predict what the computer will do and know where to look when reality differs from that prediction.

Mental model
• Modules give files explicit public imports/exports and reduce accidental global coupling.
• Throw errors for exceptional/failed operations; catch them where you can add meaning, recover, or map to a boundary.
• Avoid try/catch around everything because swallowed errors destroy diagnostic context.
• Organize small programs by responsibility so framework modules later feel like a larger version of familiar boundaries.

Step-by-step walkthrough
1. Write the concept in your own words before using a tool. If your explanation depends on framework jargon, simplify it one level.
2. Create the smallest runnable example that demonstrates only this concept. Keep it outside the main TaskFlow repository if experimentation could create noise.
3. Predict the result before running the command or clicking the UI. Prediction makes the output evidence instead of entertainment.
4. Run it and capture what actually happened: terminal output, browser state, request details, or file changes.
5. Change one assumption and repeat. Try an invalid input, wrong path, missing field, reordered data, or other safe failure relevant to the topic.
6. Explain the difference between the successful and failing runs. That explanation is the transferable skill.

TaskFlow connection
Later in the course, javascript foundations i stops being an isolated topic and becomes infrastructure for real features. When you encounter es modules, errors, and small program structure again, ask which layer owns it, what its inputs are, what output proves success, and what failure evidence is available. That prevents you from copying framework snippets without understanding the underlying browser, runtime, operating-system, or language behavior.

Guided exercise
Create a tiny example from scratch without copying the final code from a tutorial. Keep the example under about 30–50 lines where possible. After it works, deliberately break one assumption. Write the exact symptom and the smallest fix. Then delete the experiment or commit it in a dedicated practice folder so it does not pollute production project structure.

Check your understanding
• Can you describe the concept without naming a framework?
• Can you point to the exact input and output?
• Can you name one common incorrect assumption?
• Can you reproduce the idea in a tiny example?
• Can you diagnose one intentional failure using evidence rather than guesses?

Instructor note
Do not rush because the syntax looks easy. Most difficult full-stack bugs are not caused by forgetting syntax; they come from an incorrect model of ownership, execution environment, identity, time, or data flow. The foundation track exists so later lessons can move quickly without becoming mysterious.

Lab: ES Modules, Errors, and Small Program Structure

Purpose
This lab converts the previous explanation into a small piece of evidence you created yourself. Do not begin by copying the finished example. Start with the behavior you expect, then make the computer prove or disprove your model.

Your task
Split a tiny program into two ES modules, create one intentional import/export mismatch, read the runtime error, and repair it.

Working method
1. Create the smallest clean starting point.
2. Predict the first result in writing.
3. Implement only enough to test that prediction.
4. Run it and capture the result.
5. Add one intentional failure or changed assumption.
6. Diagnose from evidence before editing randomly.
7. Restore the correct behavior.
8. Close the reference and reproduce the important part from memory.

Why this is separate from the concept lesson
Reading can create familiarity without recall. The separate lab forces retrieval, execution, and debugging. Those three abilities are what later framework lessons assume when the codebase becomes larger.

Definition of done
You have a runnable example, one recorded prediction, one successful result, one controlled failure with diagnosis, and a short explain-back in your own words.
